chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, from Abu Bilal al-Makki, who said:

I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) enter al-Hijr from the side of the door. Then he stood performing salat at a distance of two cubits from the House. So I said to him: I have not seen anyone from your family pray in front of the Mizab. He said: This is the prayer place of Shabbar and Shabbir, the two sons of Harun (Aaron).

key_terms.الحجر: Hijr Ismail — the semicircular enclosure on the northwest side of the Kaaba, believed to contain the graves of Prophets Ismail and Hagar
key_terms.الميزاب: Mizab ar-Rahma — the golden water spout on the roof of the Kaaba through which rainwater drains; praying directly beneath it is considered especially meritorious
key_terms.ذراع: Cubit — a unit of measurement equal to the length of the forearm (approximately 45-50 cm)
key_terms.شبر وشبير: Shabbar and Shabbir — the Arabic/Hebrew names for the two sons of Prophet Harun (Aaron), corresponding to the Hebrew Gershom and Eliezer; they are also the pre-Islamic Arabic names of Imam al-Hasan and Imam al-Husayn
key_terms.مصلى: Prayer place or spot; the specific location designated or associated with a particular person for prayer

ai.seo_question: Where in Hijr Ismail did Imam al-Sadiq pray, and what is the significance of that spot?
ai.summary: Abu Bilal al-Makki, a companion present in Mecca, witnessed Imam al-Sadiq (AS) enter Hijr Ismail — the semicircular area adjacent to the Kaaba — from the gate side and pray at a specific spot two cubits from the Kaaba wall, not in front of the Mizab (the gold water spout on the roof of the Kaaba). When asked about this, the Imam revealed that this precise location was the ancient prayer place of Shabbar and Shabbir, the Islamic names for the two sons of Prophet Harun (Aaron). This identification connects the Imam's devotional practice to a pre-Islamic sacred tradition preserved at the Kaaba, illustrating the continuity of prophetic worship at Mecca across generations.
